newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bonn's EMU gold plan leaves budget outlook clouded.
newsitem.headline: Bonn's EMU gold plan leaves budget outlook clouded.

text.p: Germany's plan to bolster its sagging public finances by revaluing the Bundesbank's gold reserves is within the letter of European Union monetary law but not the spirit, analysts said on Friday.
"From an economic point of view it makes sense, but to use Italian-style tactics is very unseemly," one London-based economist said.
Faced with a shortfall in revenues, Germany said on Thursday it would consider revaluing its gold in order to lower the government's debt and debt-servicing costs.

At best, some say, it is a manoeuvre which is long overdue in that it is necessary ahead of the creation of a European Central Bank. Thus it is perfectly within the EU's accounting guidelines for governments struggling to qualify for monetary union.
At worst it is an embarrassing admission that "creative accounting" methods are needed for a government that has routinely criticised others for slack budgetary discipline.
Italy, which has been sharply criticised for using one-off measures to bring its 1997 budget deficit down to three percent of gross domestic product, wasted no time in pointing the finger at Bonn.

"I would be very surprised if the German government were to have recourse to accounting gimmicks such as the use of asset sales or revaluation in order to meet a revenue shortfall for 1997," Italian foreign minister Lamberto Dini said on Friday.

The difficulty in understanding how a revaluation of the Bundesbank's 95 million ounces of gold reserves would plug an 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) revenue gap stems from differences in the German government's intentions and what is possible.

As with most national central banks, annual profits -- in this case a revaluation could leave the Bundesbank with a windfall of over 40 billion marks -- are often transferred into the government's coffers.
Should the German government want to, and if the Bundesbank complied, such a transfer would have a direct impact on Bonn's 1997 deficit, the critical year for complying with Maastricht's criteria.

"Since profit transfers from the Bundesbank are counted as normal government revenues under Maastricht procedures, this operation would reduce both the government's deficit and debt ratio," says Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt of the monetary union's guiding Maastricht treaty.

But German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday said the proceeds from a revaluation would be used to reduce the large mountain of debt associated with the costs of German reunification -- the so-called Debt Heritage Fund.
EU officials say such a transfer is perfectly within the accounting guidelines and was approved by Eurostat, the EU's statistical watchdog, earlier this year.
Germany's outstanding debt level has been rising in recent years, moving above the 60 percent of GDP threshold outlined in the treaty.
At a meeting of EU finance ministers in March, Waigel outlined the dilemma Bonn faced in coping with this growing stock of debt, and his plea was accepted by all of his EU counterparts.

Logically, EU officials at the time said that if one accepted Germany's special circumstances, interest payments associated with such costs should be forgiven as well as they have a direct bearing on the deficit.
But Germany has not followed this route and it is not proposing to do so under the gold plan either. Which still leaves it with the problem of filling the gapping budget shortfall.
While a reduction in debt could help to ease the level of interest payments and, therefore, the deficit, the budget shortfall is too large to be filled in this way.

As an alternative, Waigel also proposed selling some the government's holdings in Deutsche Telekom AG earlier than expected. During the company's initial public offering, Bonn promised not to sell any of its shares before the year 2000.
But here again, if one applies the EU's accounting guidelines, a sale of shares would only be applicable to Germany's debt level, not its deficit. ($ = 1.702 German Marks)
